title: Relics, honestly
hook: Catholics honor the remains of saints as signs of holy lives, not magic

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was beatification, the step that makes someone Blessed, and your line was the long line. What did you find that was only partway done? Day nine hundred fifty.

A grandmother's wedding ring, kept in a drawer. A father's reading glasses, still on the shelf years later. A child's first shoe. Nobody thinks the ring has powers. Nobody prays to the glasses. But nobody throws them away either, because they were close to someone who mattered, and touching them brings that person near. Hold that drawer in mind. It's the honest way into a word that makes some people uneasy, the word for what Catholics keep from the saints.
screen: `A RING IN A DRAWER.` → `GLASSES STILL ON THE SHELF.` → `CLOSE TO SOMEONE WHO MATTERED.`

segments.voice: A relic is something that remains from a saint: a piece of the body, often a fragment of bone, or something the saint used or wore. Catholics keep relics in churches, in altars, in small glass cases called reliquaries, and honor them. Honor is the key word. In Catholic teaching, relics are venerated, not worshipped. Worship belongs to God alone. A relic is honored because of the person it points to, and because of what Catholics believe about the body: that it was a temple of the Holy Spirit and will rise again. The Psalms put the feeling simply, in the Douay-Rheims: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints." The Bible also has stories that sit behind the practice. In the books of Kings, a dead man is lowered into the grave of the prophet Elisha, touches his bones, and comes back to life. In the Acts of the Apostles, cloths that had touched Paul are carried to the sick, and they recover. Catholics read those as God acting through holy people, even through what they leave behind. Now the honest part. Relics have been faked, stolen, sold and fought over. The Church's own teaching warns against superstition, against treating any object as if it worked by itself, like a charm. Church law forbids selling relics at all. So a relic, rightly understood, is not a lucky object. It's closer to that drawer at home. A body, or a thing, that once belonged to someone who loved God, kept close so the memory stays warm.
screen: `WHAT REMAINS FROM A SAINT.` · `VENERATED, NOT WORSHIPPED.` · `ELISHA'S BONES, PAUL'S CLOTHS.` · `NOT A CHARM; NEVER FOR SALE.` · then, large: `PRECIOUS IN THE SIGHT OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: visit a church's relic. Some churches have one in or under the altar, or in a side chapel; when you can, go and stand in front of it for a minute. For now, in the sit, think of an object you've kept because of someone you loved. See it clearly: its weight, its color, where it lives in your home. Let the person come to mind through it. If you pray, you can pray for them, or ask a saint to pray with you. If not, hold the object and the person together, quietly. The bell holds the time.
Relic. Something that remains from a saint, their body or something they used, honored for the holy life it points to, never worshipped.
Your line: bodies that loved god. Today, treat one ordinary body with honor, your own included: a rest, a meal eaten slowly, a hand held. Day nine hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Catholic churches often keep relics of saints in altars or reliquaries; on feast days relics may be exposed for veneration, and people may kneel, pray nearby or touch the reliquary, while Church law forbids selling relics.

fork.reveal: Church law forbids selling relics at all. the practice is about honoring a holy life, not trading in objects.

original.note: Latin: remains, what is left behind; the word Catholics use for the relics of saints.

notes: Confirm canon 1190 §1 (it is absolutely forbidden to sell sacred relics) and CCC 2111 on superstition; CCC 1674 lists veneration of relics among forms of popular piety.
The 'temple of the Holy Spirit' and resurrection of the body are given as the reasons Catholics honor bodies; confirm framing.
Statement that relics 'have been faked, stolen, sold and fought over' is general history, no specific claim; confirm tone is acceptable.
